mcqs.question: Why can a single forward pass classify every existing interval into "before", "overlapping", or "after" the new interval without ever revisiting an earlier zone?
options: Because the new interval is always inserted at either the very start or very end of the list
Because overlapping intervals are removed from the list before the pass begins
Because the existing list is already sorted, so once the scan leaves the "before" zone it can never re-enter it, and the same holds moving from "overlapping" to "after"
Because every existing interval is guaranteed to overlap the new one
mcqs.explanation: The sortedness of the input is what guarantees the scan only ever moves forward through the three zones — once an interval's end passes the new interval's start, everything before it is truly done, and once an interval's start passes the new interval's end, everything from there is truly untouched. Nothing about the new interval's position or overlap count is assumed.

mcqs.question: Appending the new interval to the list and re-running Merge Intervals on the whole thing produces a correct result. Why is it still considered a weaker answer to "Insert Interval"?
options: It doesn't handle the case where the new interval overlaps multiple existing intervals
It requires a linked list instead of an array
It fails when the existing list has more than one interval
It pays an unnecessary O(n log n) re-sort on a list that the problem already guarantees is sorted, when an O(n) single pass would do
mcqs.explanation: The append-then-merge approach is correct but ignores the given precondition that the existing list is already sorted and merged — re-sorting it is pure wasted work compared to the O(n) three-zone pass. It handles multiple overlaps and any list length just fine; the issue is purely complexity, not correctness.

mcqs.question: A buggy Insert Interval implementation correctly builds the "before" and merged "overlapping" zones but omits the final loop over the remaining index range. What's the resulting bug?
options: It silently drops every existing interval that comes after the merge window, but only when the new interval doesn't happen to touch the last few entries
It duplicates the last existing interval in the output
It throws an index-out-of-range error on every input
It merges intervals that shouldn't be merged, producing an output that's too short
mcqs.explanation: Without a final loop flushing the remaining "after" zone, any interval sitting after the merge window never gets copied to the result and is silently lost. The bug hides in test cases where the new interval overlaps the last existing interval, since there's no tail left to forget in that case.

mcqs.question: For a calendar with 10,000 already-merged events receiving frequent single-event inserts, what's the practical cost of choosing append-then-remerge over the three-zone single pass?
options: The three-zone pass exploits the existing sorted order and costs roughly O(n), while append-then-remerge re-sorts on every insert at roughly O(n log n) — over 10x more work per insert at this scale
There's no practical difference since both are O(n log n) once sorting is involved
Append-then-remerge is actually faster in practice because sorting is highly optimized in most languages
The difference only matters if the calendar has fewer than 100 events
mcqs.explanation: At 10,000 elements, log n is roughly 13, so re-sorting costs on the order of 130,000 comparison-scale operations versus roughly 10,000 for the direct pass — a real, growing gap, not a rounding error. Neither claim about "no difference" or "faster in practice" holds; the whole point of exploiting the sorted precondition is avoiding that repeated multiplier.

mcqs.question: Does inserting in place (shifting the tail of the array to make room) improve Insert Interval's asymptotic complexity over building a fresh result array?
options: Yes — in-place insertion is always O(log n) because no new array is allocated
Yes — it eliminates the need to scan the "before" zone entirely
No — shifting the tail still costs O(n) per insert, so it saves allocation overhead but not asymptotic complexity; only a different structure like an interval tree changes the complexity class
No — in-place insertion is actually slower because it requires two full passes instead of one
mcqs.explanation: Shifting elements to insert in place is still an O(n) operation per insert, same complexity class as building a fresh array — it can reduce allocation churn but doesn't change the asymptotic picture. Getting to O(log n) insert and query requires switching data structures entirely, such as an interval tree or balanced BST.
